title: Anxiety Treatment in Maryland: Signs, Therapy, and When to Get Help
description: Learn the signs of anxiety in adults and teens, what outpatient therapy and medication management look like, and when to reach out for help in Maryland.
shortAnswer: Feeling anxious is a normal part of life. For people with an anxiety disorder, the worry does not go away and can get worse over time. Anxiety disorders are usually treated with therapy, medicine, or both, and a clinician makes the diagnosis.
keyTakeaways: Anxiety becomes a concern when it lasts, spreads to many situations, or gets in the way of school, work, or relationships.
Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a well-studied therapy for anxiety, and medicine is another option.
Finding the right treatment can take some trial and error, and both therapy and medicine can take time to work.
Do not stop a prescribed medicine on your own. Talk with your provider first.

sections.heading: What anxiety is, and when it becomes a disorder
paragraphs: Anxiety is a feeling of fear, dread, and unease. It is often a normal response to stress, and it can even help you focus. MedlinePlus explains that in an anxiety disorder, the anxiety does not go away.

The National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) says about one-third of U.S. adolescents and adults have an anxiety disorder at some point in their lives. Common types include generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, and phobia-related disorders.
Only a clinician can tell you whether you have an anxiety disorder. This page is for general education and is not a diagnosis.

sections.heading: Signs to watch for
paragraphs: In adults, generalized anxiety disorder can look like excessive worry about everyday things such as work, health, money, or family. People may also feel on edge, restless, irritable, tired, or have trouble concentrating or sleeping. Physical signs can include headaches, muscle aches, stomachaches, trembling, or sweating.

In children and teens, worries often center on school, friendships, and the future. They may fear making mistakes or letting others down, and may try to be perfect to cope. With social anxiety, teens may avoid school, have trouble making friends, or complain of stomachaches or headaches.
Panic attacks are sudden waves of intense fear. They can bring a pounding heart, sweating, trembling, trouble breathing, or dizziness. NIMH notes that they are distressing but not life-threatening.
Avoiding places or activities you used to do is another sign. Caffeine, other substances, and some medicines can make anxiety symptoms worse, according to MedlinePlus.

sections.heading: What outpatient treatment can look like
paragraphs: NIMH says anxiety disorders are usually treated with psychotherapy (talk therapy), medicine, or both. Cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT, is well studied and described by NIMH as a gold-standard psychotherapy. It teaches new ways of thinking and reacting. For some people it includes exposure therapy, which helps them slowly face situations they have been avoiding. Acceptance and commitment therapy is another option.

Medicines can include antidepressants such as SSRIs and SNRIs, which can take several weeks to work (NIMH lists about 4 to 8 weeks for antidepressants). Buspirone is taken daily and needs 3 to 4 weeks to work. Benzodiazepines may be used for short-term relief of severe anxiety, but long-term use can lead to tolerance or dependence, so they are usually prescribed for short periods.
NIMH says finding the best treatment may take trial and error. Habits like exercise, sleep, and cutting back on caffeine can help, but they do not replace treatment.

At King Health Systems, outpatient care can include individual, family, and group therapy, psychiatric evaluation and medication management with psychiatric nurse practitioners, and psychiatric rehabilitation program (PRP) services. Telehealth is available during our office hours, Monday to Friday, 9 to 5. We accept Maryland Medicaid.

sections.heading: What a first visit may involve
paragraphs: NIMH says a provider may ask when your symptoms began, how long they have lasted, how often they happen, and how they affect your life. A physical exam may be used to rule out another cause, and MedlinePlus notes that a psychological evaluation is part of the process.

If medicine is discussed, tell your provider about all other medicines, vitamins, supplements, and allergies, and about any past problems with medicines. Ask how to take it and what side effects to expect.
Treatment decisions depend on your needs and preferences. You can ask questions at any point.

sections.heading: Medicine safety and sticking with a plan
paragraphs: NIMH advises against stopping a prescribed medicine on your own, even if you feel better. Your provider can lower the dose slowly and safely.
Contact your provider right away if you have problems with a medicine or think it may be doing more harm than good.

faqs.q: How do I know if my anxiety is more than normal stress?
faqs.a: Anxiety is a concern when it does not go away, shows up in many situations, gets worse over time, or interferes with school, work, or relationships. A clinician can help you sort out what is going on.

faqs.q: What is CBT?
faqs.a: Cognitive behavioral therapy is a type of talk therapy. NIMH describes it as a well-studied treatment for anxiety that teaches new ways of thinking and reacting. It may include exposure therapy, which helps people gradually face situations they avoid.

faqs.q: Will I need medicine?
faqs.a: Not always. NIMH says treatment is usually therapy, medicine, or both, and the choice depends on your needs and preferences. A psychiatric provider can talk through the options with you.

faqs.q: Can teens get help for anxiety too?
faqs.a: Yes. NIMH says social anxiety disorder usually starts in childhood or adolescence, and CBT is a common treatment for social anxiety disorder. KHS serves children 5 and older, teens, adults, and families.

whenToGetHelp: Consider reaching out if anxiety lasts, keeps getting worse, or interferes with school, work, or relationships. If you or someone you know is struggling or having thoughts of suicide, call or text 988 (the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline). In a life-threatening emergency, call 911. To talk with King Health Systems about care, call 410-578-4340.

title: Depression Treatment in Maryland: Signs, Therapy, and Medication Options
description: Learn the signs of depression, how outpatient therapy and medication management work, and when to get help. For children, teens, and adults in Maryland.
shortAnswer: Depression is more than feeling sad for a short time. It can change how you think, feel, sleep, eat, and handle daily life. Outpatient care, such as talk therapy and medication management, is a common way to get help, and a clinician can tell you what fits your needs.
keyTakeaways: Depression does not always look like sadness. It can show up as irritability, tiredness, aches, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy.
Treatment often includes talk therapy, medicine, or both. A clinician makes the diagnosis and works with you on a plan.
Medicines can take weeks to work, and you should not stop them without talking to your provider.
If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, call or text 988 right away. In an emergency, call 911.

sections.heading: What depression is
paragraphs: Everyone feels sad or low sometimes, and these feelings usually pass with time. Depression, also called major depressive disorder, is different. It can cause severe symptoms that affect how a person feels, thinks, and handles daily life, including sleeping, eating, and working (NIMH).

Depression is common. A CDC survey found that 13.1% of people ages 12 and older had depression in the past 2 weeks, based on data from August 2021 to August 2023. The rate was highest among ages 12 to 19 (19.2%) and lowest among adults 60 and older (8.7%). If you are struggling, you are not alone.

sections.heading: Signs to watch for
paragraphs: Signs of depression differ from person to person and do not always look like sadness. MedlinePlus lists common signs such as feeling sad, empty, hopeless, irritable, anxious, or guilty; losing interest in activities you used to enjoy; changes in appetite or sleep; ongoing tiredness; aches, pains, or digestive problems; pulling away from family and friends; and thoughts of death or suicide.

Children and teens may seem irritable rather than sad. Younger children may seem anxious or cranky, pretend to be sick, refuse to go to school, or cling to a parent. Older children and teens may have trouble at school, feel easily frustrated or restless, or have low self-esteem (NIMH). AACAP also notes that children may have more physical complaints, such as frequent headaches or stomachaches.

Only a clinician can diagnose depression. For a diagnosis, NIMH explains that symptoms usually last most of the day, nearly every day, for at least 2 weeks. People with only a few symptoms may still benefit from treatment.

sections.heading: What outpatient treatment can look like
paragraphs: Treatment for depression often combines talk therapy and medicine. Talk therapy (psychotherapy) helps you notice and change troubling thoughts, feelings, and behaviors. It can be one-on-one or in a group (MedlinePlus). Two common types are cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), which helps people challenge unhelpful thoughts and behaviors, and interpersonal therapy (IPT), which focuses on relationships and life events that affect mood (NIMH).
For children and teens, AACAP describes CBT and IPT as effective options. Care can also include family meetings and, with permission, working with the child's school.

Medicine, such as antidepressants, may also be part of a plan. NIMH says antidepressants usually take about 4 to 8 weeks to work, and sleep, appetite, and concentration often improve before mood does. MedlinePlus notes it may take several tries to find the right one, and that side effects can happen. Do not stop a medicine on your own. Talk with your provider first.

NIMH also says children, teens, and young adults under 25 may have more suicidal thoughts or behavior, especially in the first few weeks of an antidepressant or after a dose change, so close monitoring is advised. Tell your provider right away about any new or worsening thoughts of self-harm.

At King Health Systems, outpatient options include individual, family, and group therapy, psychiatric evaluation and medication management, and the Psychiatric Rehabilitation Program (PRP). Our offices are open Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., and we accept Maryland Medicaid. Call us to ask about telehealth or in-person visits.

sections.heading: What a first visit may involve
paragraphs: At a first visit, a provider may ask when your symptoms began, how long they have lasted, how often they happen, and whether they keep you from doing your usual activities (NIMH). Writing down your symptoms before the visit can help.
A provider may also check for other causes that can look like depression, such as certain medicines, viruses, or thyroid problems, using an exam, an interview, and sometimes lab tests (NIMH).

You and the clinician can then talk about options and make a plan together. You can ask questions at any time, including about how long treatment may take, what side effects to expect, and how family members can help.

sections.heading: Taking the next step
paragraphs: MedlinePlus advises seeing a health care provider or mental health professional if you think you may be depressed, or if someone you care about may be. For children and teens, AACAP says to get help if sadness, irritability, or loss of interest continues day after day. A pediatrician, school counselor, or mental health professional can help connect your child with someone who can do a full assessment.

Habits like regular exercise, a steady sleep schedule, and managing stress can have long-term benefits for mental health, but most cases of depression cannot be prevented (MedlinePlus). Treatment is a personal process, and no one can promise how any one person will respond.

faqs.q: Is depression the same as being sad?
faqs.a: No. Everyone feels sad sometimes, and those feelings usually pass. Depression is more severe and lasts longer, and it can affect sleep, eating, work, and daily life (NIMH). A clinician can help tell the difference.

faqs.q: How long do antidepressants take to work?
faqs.a: NIMH says they usually take about 4 to 8 weeks to work, and some symptoms like sleep and appetite may improve first. It may take several tries to find the right medicine. Do not stop taking it without talking to your provider.

faqs.q: Can children and teens get depression?
faqs.a: Yes. AACAP states that more than one in seven teens experience depression each year. Young people may show it as irritability, trouble at school, pulling away from friends, or physical complaints like stomachaches and headaches.

faqs.q: Do I need medicine, or can I do therapy only?
faqs.a: Treatment often includes talk therapy, medicine, or both (MedlinePlus). A clinician will talk with you about the options and help you choose a plan that fits your needs.

whenToGetHelp: If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide or is in crisis, call or text 988 (the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) right away, or chat at 988lifeline.org. In a life-threatening emergency, call 911. If sadness, irritability, or loss of interest keeps going day after day, or gets in the way of school, work, or home life, reach out to a clinician. King Health Systems can be reached at 410-578-4340. This page is for education only and is not a diagnosis; a clinician makes diagnoses.

title: Trauma and PTSD: Signs and Treatment Options in Maryland
description: Learn the signs of trauma and PTSD, the talk therapies and medicines used to treat it, and when to seek outpatient help in Maryland.
shortAnswer: PTSD is a mental health condition that some people develop after living through or seeing a frightening or life-threatening event. Talk therapy, medicine, or both are the main treatments, and a trained clinician is the one who can make a diagnosis. If symptoms last longer than a month or get in the way of daily life, it is a good time to reach out.
keyTakeaways: Feeling shaken after a scary event is common, and most people feel better over time. Symptoms that last more than a month or disrupt daily life are a reason to talk with a professional.
PTSD symptoms fall into four groups: reliving the event, avoiding reminders, negative changes in thoughts and mood, and feeling on edge.
The VA National Center for PTSD lists trauma-focused talk therapies, such as Cognitive Processing Therapy, Prolonged Exposure, and EMDR, as having the most research support.
Only a mental health professional can diagnose PTSD. In a crisis, call or text 988; in an emergency, call 911.

sections.heading: What trauma and PTSD are
paragraphs: Many people feel upset, jumpy, or sad after a frightening event. The VA National Center for PTSD says these stress reactions are normal and that most people feel better within a few weeks.

PTSD, or post-traumatic stress disorder, is a mental health condition that some people develop after going through or seeing an event such as an assault, an accident, a disaster, or combat. According to NIMH, it can affect anyone at any age, and learning that a close friend or relative went through trauma can also lead to it.
NIMH reports that roughly 6 in 100 people will have PTSD at some point in their lives. PTSD affects people differently, and symptoms may start later or come and go.

sections.heading: Signs to watch for
paragraphs: NIMH and MedlinePlus describe four kinds of symptoms. The first is reliving the event, such as flashbacks, bad dreams, or frightening thoughts. The second is avoidance, which means staying away from places, people, or thoughts that remind you of what happened.

The third is changes in thinking and mood. This can include negative beliefs about yourself or the world, guilt or blame, losing interest in things you used to enjoy, or feeling numb. The fourth is feeling on edge, such as being easily startled, having trouble sleeping or concentrating, or having angry outbursts.

In children and teens, NIMH notes that signs can look different. Children under 6 may wet the bed after being toilet trained, act out the event in play, or become unusually clingy. Older children and teens may show more adult-like symptoms, along with disruptive behavior.

NIMH says symptoms must last more than a month and interfere with daily life, such as work or relationships, to meet the criteria for PTSD. A clinician makes the diagnosis. This page cannot tell you or your child whether PTSD is present.

sections.heading: What outpatient treatment can look like
paragraphs: NIMH and MedlinePlus say the main treatments are talk therapy (psychotherapy), medicine, or both. Many people receive care in outpatient settings, which means regular visits while living at home.

The VA National Center for PTSD says trauma-focused therapies have the most research support. These include Cognitive Processing Therapy, which helps you reframe negative thoughts about the trauma; Prolonged Exposure, which helps you gradually face feelings and activities you have avoided; and EMDR, which helps you process the trauma while focusing on a back-and-forth movement or sound.

NIMH explains that therapy can be done one-on-one or in groups and often lasts 6 to 12 weeks or longer. For medicine, NIMH says the FDA has approved two antidepressants of the SSRI type for PTSD, and other medicines may be used for problems like sleep or nightmares. The VA says benzodiazepines are not recommended for PTSD.

At King Health Systems, care can include individual, family, and group therapy, psychiatric evaluation and medication management, and PRP (Psychiatric Rehabilitation Program) services. Which treatment fits you or your child is a decision you make together with your clinician. Results differ from person to person, and no treatment can promise a particular outcome.

sections.heading: What a first visit may involve
paragraphs: A first visit is usually a conversation. A clinician asks about what has been happening, your symptoms, your sleep, your health, and what support you have. You do not have to share every detail of a traumatic event to get started, and you can go at a pace that feels manageable.

The clinician may talk with you about treatment options, including talk therapy and whether a medicine evaluation makes sense. For children and teens, parents or caregivers are often part of the conversation.

You can ask questions at any time, such as what a therapy involves, how long it may last, and what to do between visits. The VA suggests choosing a treatment with your provider by weighing benefits, risks, side effects, and your own preferences.

sections.heading: Other ways to cope and find support
paragraphs: NIMH says that when symptoms do not improve after 6 to 8 weeks, it is worth talking with a health care provider, so tell your clinician if you are not seeing progress. The VA also encourages people to take an active part in their treatment.
For children and teens, NIMH suggests talking with a parent, school counselor, or health care provider when behavior changes last weeks or months and interfere with home, school, or friendships.

faqs.q: Does everyone who goes through trauma get PTSD?
faqs.a: No. The VA National Center for PTSD says stress reactions after a frightening event are normal and most people feel better within a few weeks. NIMH reports that roughly 6 in 100 people will have PTSD at some point in their lives.

faqs.q: How long do symptoms have to last before I should get help?
faqs.a: The VA says to talk with a doctor or mental health provider if symptoms last longer than a month, are very upsetting, or disrupt daily life. MedlinePlus also links symptoms lasting longer than four weeks to possible PTSD. You can reach out sooner if you are worried.

faqs.q: Is talk therapy or medicine better?
faqs.a: NIMH says treatment can be talk therapy, medicine, or both. The VA says trauma-focused talk therapies have the most research support. A clinician can help you choose based on your needs and preferences.

faqs.q: Can children and teens get help for trauma?
faqs.a: Yes. NIMH describes how PTSD signs can look in children and teens, and suggests talking with a parent, school counselor, or health care provider if behavior changes last weeks or months. King Health Systems serves children age 5 and older, teens, adults, and families.

whenToGetHelp: Reach out if upsetting symptoms last longer than a month, cause a lot of distress, or get in the way of work, school, sleep, or relationships. King Health Systems can be reached at 410-578-4340 (telehealth available Monday to Friday, 9 to 5; Medicaid accepted). If you or someone you know is in crisis or having thoughts of suicide, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline). If there is immediate danger, call 911.

title: ADHD in Children, Teens and Adults: Signs, Evaluation and Treatment in Maryland
description: Learn the signs of ADHD in kids, teens and adults, how an evaluation works, and treatment options like behavioral therapy and medication.
shortAnswer: ADHD is a condition that affects attention, activity levels and impulse control. It often starts in childhood and can continue into adulthood. A trained clinician makes the diagnosis after a careful evaluation, and treatment often includes behavioral therapy, medication, or both.
keyTakeaways: ADHD involves ongoing inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity that show up in more than one setting, such as home and school or work.
There is no single test for ADHD. A clinician looks at history, behavior reports and symptom checklists, and checks for other conditions that can look similar.
There is no cure, but treatment can reduce symptoms and improve daily life. Common options are behavioral therapy, parent training, medication, or a combination.
Adults can be diagnosed too. It is not too late to ask for an evaluation.

sections.heading: What ADHD is
paragraphs: ADHD stands for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. The National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) describes it as a neurodevelopmental disorder marked by inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity. Everyone is distracted or fidgety at times. ADHD is considered when these behaviors happen often, show up in several settings, and get in the way of daily life.

The exact cause is not known. MedlinePlus says ADHD likely comes from a mix of genetic and environmental factors. ADHD is usually first diagnosed in childhood and often continues into adulthood, and some people are not diagnosed until they are adults.

sections.heading: Signs to watch for
paragraphs: Inattention can look like careless mistakes, trouble staying focused, seeming not to listen when spoken to, not finishing tasks, poor organization, losing things often, and forgetting daily activities. Hyperactivity and impulsivity can look like fidgeting, leaving a seat when staying seated is expected, talking a lot, blurting out answers, trouble waiting a turn, and interrupting others.

In children, hyperactivity and impulsivity are often the most common signs, such as running or climbing at the wrong times. As schoolwork and social demands grow, inattention often becomes more noticeable and can affect grades and friendships, according to NIMH. In teens, hyperactivity often decreases and may look more like restlessness, while inattention and impulsivity usually continue. NIMH also notes that teens with ADHD are more likely to take impulsive risks, such as substance use.

In adults, NIMH lists signs such as inattention, restlessness, impulsivity, irritability, low frustration tolerance and frequent mood changes. For an adult diagnosis, symptoms must have started in childhood, even if they were never recognized then. ADHD can also occur alongside other concerns, including anxiety, depression, sleep problems and learning disorders, which can make it harder to sort out.

sections.heading: How an ADHD evaluation works
paragraphs: The CDC says there is no single test for ADHD. Diagnosis takes several steps. The CDC says a mental health professional, such as a psychologist or psychiatrist, or a primary care provider can make the diagnosis. Only a qualified clinician can diagnose ADHD. This page cannot tell you whether you or your child has it.

According to NIMH, the clinician reviews mental health and medical history, asks about current and childhood behavior and school experiences, and, with permission, may gather information from family members and teachers. The clinician may use rating scales or symptom checklists. Psychological tests may be used to look at thinking skills and to rule out learning disabilities. The CDC adds that a medical exam, including hearing and vision checks, can help rule out other causes.

To meet the criteria described by NIMH and MedlinePlus, symptoms must have begun before age 12, lasted at least 6 months, appeared in two or more settings, and caused problems at school, at work or socially. The clinician also checks whether another condition, such as anxiety, depression, a sleep disorder or stress, could better explain the symptoms.

sections.heading: What outpatient treatment can look like
paragraphs: NIMH and MedlinePlus both say there is no cure for ADHD, but treatment can reduce symptoms and improve daily functioning. Plans often combine approaches, and good plans include close follow-up and changes over time.

Behavioral therapy helps change behavior through practical steps, such as organizing tasks, building social skills and self-monitoring. NIMH says cognitive behavioral therapy can build skills for focus, organization and breaking tasks into smaller steps. For children and teens, parents play an active role in therapy, and parent training can help families. The CDC says parent training in behavior management is recommended as the first step for children under 6, and that for children 6 and older, medication combined with behavior therapy is recommended. Family therapy can also help families manage disruptive behavior and improve how they interact.

Medication is another option. NIMH says stimulants are the most common type and are considered highly effective, and that they must be prescribed and monitored by a provider. The CDC lists reduced appetite and trouble sleeping among possible side effects. Finding the right medicine or dose can take more than one try, so a provider needs to watch how a person responds and adjust. Talk with the prescriber about any other medicines you take.

School support can help too. MedlinePlus mentions school behavior management plans, and NIMH describes accommodations such as extra test time through a 504 Plan or an Individualized Education Program (IEP). For adults, NIMH says coaching, regular exercise, good sleep habits and time-management tools may help.

sections.heading: What a first visit may involve
paragraphs: A first visit is usually a conversation. Expect questions about your or your child's concerns, when they started, where they show up (home, school, work, with friends), and your health and family history. For a child or teen, a clinician may ask parents or guardians, and sometimes teachers, to share their observations. It can help to bring school reports, past evaluations, a list of current medicines, and notes about examples you have seen.

King Health Systems offers psychiatric evaluation and medication management, as well as individual, family and group therapy, and Psychiatric Rehabilitation Program (PRP) services. Visits can be in person or by telehealth, Monday through Friday, 9 to 5. We serve children 5 and older, teens, adults and families, accept Maryland Medicaid, and have offices in Baltimore, Laurel and Cockeysville. A clinician decides what care fits each person after talking with them.

faqs.q: Can adults have ADHD?
faqs.a: Yes. NIMH says adults can be diagnosed at any age, though symptoms must have started in childhood. Some adults were not diagnosed earlier because their symptoms were mild, were not recognized, or they coped until adult demands increased. NIMH says it is never too late to seek an evaluation.

faqs.q: Is there a test that proves ADHD?
faqs.a: No. The CDC says there is no single test. A clinician reviews history, gathers reports about behavior in different settings, and rules out other conditions that can look similar. NIMH adds that rating scales or symptom checklists may be used.

faqs.q: Does ADHD always need medication?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Treatment plans vary. The CDC says behavior therapy with parent training is the recommended first step for children under 6, while for children 6 and older medication plus behavior therapy is recommended. The right plan depends on the person, and you decide on it together with a prescriber.

faqs.q: Can ADHD be cured?
faqs.a: No. NIMH and MedlinePlus say there is no cure, but treatment can reduce symptoms and help people function better at home, at school and at work.

whenToGetHelp: Consider reaching out if attention, activity or impulsive behavior is frequent, shows up in more than one setting, and causes problems at school, work, home or in relationships. A primary care provider or a mental health clinic can start the conversation. If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide or is in emotional crisis, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline). If there is immediate danger or a medical emergency, call 911. To ask about care at King Health Systems, call 410-578-4340.

title: Mental Health Care for Children and Teens in Maryland
description: Warning signs parents notice, how outpatient therapy with family involvement works, and when to seek help for a child or teen in Maryland.
shortAnswer: Many children have fears, worries, or hard moods from time to time. It is worth getting help when signs last weeks or months and get in the way of home, school, or friendships. A clinician makes any diagnosis, and treatment often involves the whole family.
keyTakeaways: Signs that last weeks or months and disrupt home, school, or friendships are a reason to contact a health professional.
Starting treatment earlier can make it more effective.
Therapy for younger children often involves parents or caregivers, while teens may work more directly with the therapist.
A pediatrician, family doctor, or school counselor can be a first step, and KHS accepts Maryland Medicaid.

sections.heading: Signs to watch for
paragraphs: Many children sometimes have fears, worries, or disruptive behavior. The CDC says a condition becomes a concern when symptoms are severe and last, and when they interfere with school, home, or play. Symptoms can change as a child grows.
NIMH lists signs to watch for in younger children, such as frequent tantrums, being very irritable much of the time, frequent fear or worry, and unexplained stomachaches or headaches.
In older children and teens, NIMH lists losing interest in activities they used to enjoy, pulling away from friends or family, self-harm, substance use, and thoughts of suicide.
These signs do not mean a child has a particular condition. Only a trained clinician can make a diagnosis after an evaluation.

sections.heading: When to seek help
paragraphs: NIMH advises contacting a health professional when signs last weeks or months and interfere with daily life at home, at school, or with friends. It also says that the earlier treatment starts, the more effective it can be.

If you are not sure where to start, NIMH suggests talking with a pediatrician, family doctor, or school counselor. The CDC also recommends a comprehensive evaluation by a health care provider or mental health specialist to find out what is going on and which treatments fit.
A health care provider can also help rule out other health factors that may be adding to symptoms.

sections.heading: What outpatient treatment can look like
paragraphs: Outpatient care means a child lives at home and visits a clinic for appointments. According to the CDC, psychological therapy can treat a condition or teach coping skills, and it can be one-on-one or in a group. For young children, parents or caregivers are often directly involved. Older children and teens may work more directly with the therapist.

AACAP describes family therapy as a way to improve how a family functions by looking at communication patterns and offering support and education. Sessions can include the child, parents, siblings, and other relatives. The CDC notes that parent training teaches parents skills to manage a child's behavior and practice them with the child.

The CDC says behavior therapy and cognitive-behavior therapy (CBT) are the approaches most likely to reduce symptoms of common childhood conditions such as behavior problems, anxiety, and depression. CBT helps children notice their thoughts and feelings and change unhelpful thoughts and reactions.
The CDC says therapy may be combined with medication, depending on the type and severity of the problem. AACAP describes therapy as not a quick fix, and progress takes time.
At King Health Systems, care includes individual, family, and group therapy, psychiatric evaluation and medication management, and PRP. Which services fit your child is decided with a clinician.

sections.heading: What a first visit may involve
paragraphs: AACAP describes a child psychiatric evaluation as involving the child and the parents or guardians. The clinician asks about current problems, health and family history, development, school, friendships, and family relationships.
With your permission, the clinician may contact others, such as a family doctor or school staff, to learn more. AACAP says an evaluation usually takes a few hours, spread over one or more visits.
Afterward, families have time to ask questions. If a treatable problem is found, AACAP says the clinician gives recommendations and develops a treatment plan.

It can help to ask a therapist how parents or caregivers will be involved, how long treatment may take, and how progress will be checked. KHS can tell you which visit formats are available when you call.

sections.heading: School and family support
paragraphs: The CDC says parents, doctors, teachers, coaches, therapists, and family members should coordinate care. NIMH lists school counselors as a possible first contact.

The CDC also notes that healthy habits may help reduce symptoms alongside needed treatment. These include regular physical activity, a healthful diet, enough sleep for the child's age, and strong relationships with family and friends.
NIMH points families to the U.S. Department of Education for information about school accommodations and services for children with disabilities.

faqs.q: How do I know if it is a phase or something more?
faqs.a: The CDC says many children have occasional fears, worries, or disruptive behavior. It becomes a concern when symptoms are severe, last, and interfere with school, home, or play. NIMH advises contacting a health professional if signs last weeks or months. A clinician can help sort this out.

faqs.q: Will I be part of my child's therapy?
faqs.a: Often, yes. The CDC says parents or caregivers are often directly involved when children are young, and older children and teens may work more directly with the therapist. Ask the therapist how you will be involved.

faqs.q: Does my child need medication?
faqs.a: Not always. The CDC says therapy may be combined with medication depending on the type and severity of the problem. At KHS, psychiatric evaluation and medication management are offered, and a clinician can discuss whether medication is part of a plan.

faqs.q: Does KHS accept Medicaid for children and teens?
faqs.a: KHS is a Maryland Medicaid-only outpatient clinic and serves children, teens, adults, and families. Call 410-578-4340 to ask about getting started.

whenToGetHelp: If your child or someone else is in crisis or having thoughts of suicide, call or text 988 (the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) right away. If there is immediate danger or a medical emergency, call 911. For non-urgent questions or to ask about care for your child or teen, King Health Systems can be reached at 410-578-4340.

title: Mental Health Care for Adults 55 and Older in Maryland
description: Learn the signs of depression, anxiety, grief, and loneliness in adults 55+, and how outpatient and telehealth care in Maryland can help.
shortAnswer: Mental health matters at every age. Life changes such as illness, losing a loved one, or feeling alone can lead to depression or anxiety, and these conditions can be treated. If symptoms last or get in the way of daily life, talk with a health care provider or a mental health clinician.
keyTakeaways: Serious illness, losing a loved one, and ongoing loneliness can affect mental health at any age, including after 55.
Mental health conditions can be treated with talk therapy, medication, or both.
Telehealth lets you meet with a provider by video or phone without travel, if you have a device and internet or phone service.
If symptoms last or interfere with daily life, reach out. You do not have to wait until things feel unbearable.

sections.heading: Why mental health matters after 55
paragraphs: The National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) says mental health is important at every stage of life. Life changes such as a serious illness or the loss of a loved one can affect how you feel.

When grief, social isolation, or loneliness do not ease, they can lead to conditions such as depression and anxiety. The CDC also lists chronic illness, long-term disability, losing a loved one, and limited transportation as things that can raise the risk of isolation and loneliness. It notes that older adults are more at risk for social isolation.

The CDC explains the difference this way: social isolation is when a person does not have relationships or contact with others, and loneliness is feeling alone or disconnected from others. Both are linked to a higher risk of depression and anxiety, among other health problems.

sections.heading: Signs to watch for
paragraphs: NIMH lists these warning signs: changes in mood, energy, or appetite; trouble sleeping; trouble concentrating; more worry than usual; irritability; ongoing headaches, stomach problems, or pain; using more alcohol or drugs; feeling sad or hopeless; and thoughts of death or suicide.

Some of these signs can also come from a physical health problem. A health care provider can help find out whether a physical cause is part of the picture. Only a clinician can diagnose a mental health condition.

Grief is a normal reaction to loss. MedlinePlus says it can show up as anger, guilt, anxiety, sadness, sleep problems, or changes in appetite. Talk with a provider if these feelings are hard to manage or are affecting your health or daily life.

sections.heading: What outpatient treatment can look like
paragraphs: NIMH describes psychotherapy (talk therapy) and medication as the most common forms of mental health treatment. Therapy can be used alone or together with medication, and a mental health professional can help you choose a plan that fits your needs.

Talk therapy helps people notice and change troubling emotions, thoughts, and behaviors. It is usually one-on-one with a licensed professional, and it can also be done in a group. It may include coping and problem-solving skills, relaxation, and supportive counseling. Research shows many types of therapy reduce symptoms of depression and anxiety.

Medications such as antidepressants may be part of a plan. NIMH says finding the right medication may take several tries and some medications take weeks to work. Tell your provider about every medicine, vitamin, and supplement you take, and ask about side effects. Do not stop a prescribed medicine on your own, even if you feel better. Your provider can lower the dose safely.

At King Health Systems, outpatient care includes individual, family, and group therapy, psychiatric evaluation and medication management with psychiatric nurse practitioners, and Psychiatric Rehabilitation Program (PRP) services. We accept Maryland Medicaid.

sections.heading: Care by telehealth
paragraphs: NIMH explains that virtual care can include video calls or phone calls. Services can include an assessment, therapy, medication prescriptions, and regular check-ins. NIMH says virtual care can be effective for conditions such as anxiety, depression, and PTSD.

Benefits include no travel, more flexible scheduling, and access for people who cannot easily get to in-person care. Drawbacks include needing a device and an internet connection, and privacy concerns if others can see or overhear the visit. A quiet, private space helps.
King Health Systems offers telehealth Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Ask our team whether a telehealth visit is a good fit for you.

sections.heading: What a first visit may involve
paragraphs: At a first visit, a clinician will usually ask how you have been feeling, what has changed in your life, how you are sleeping and eating, and what health conditions and medicines you have. This helps the clinician understand your needs and suggest next steps.

You can ask questions about the clinician's training, their approach to treatment, what to expect, and how your information is kept private. Together you can decide on a plan, which may include therapy, a psychiatric evaluation, or both.
It can help to bring a list of your medicines and any notes about what you have noticed. You can also bring a trusted family member or friend if you would like support.

faqs.q: Is feeling down or worried part of getting older?
faqs.a: Life changes can be hard at any age, but persistent sadness, worry, or hopelessness is not something you have to just live with. NIMH says mental health conditions can be treated, and that recognizing the signs and seeing a health care provider are the first steps.

faqs.q: Can talk therapy help, or do I need medication?
faqs.a: NIMH says psychotherapy can be used alone or with medication. The right plan depends on your needs, and a mental health professional can help you decide.

faqs.q: I feel lonely but I do not feel sad. Does it matter?
faqs.a: Yes. The CDC says social isolation and loneliness are linked to health risks, including depression and anxiety. Isolation can affect health even when a person does not feel lonely. Talking with a clinician can be a good step.

faqs.q: Can I get care by phone or video?
faqs.a: King Health Systems offers telehealth Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Telehealth needs a device and a phone or internet connection, so ask our team what would work for you.

whenToGetHelp: Reach out to a provider if symptoms last, get worse, or interfere with sleep, eating, relationships, or daily life. If you or someone you know is in crisis or thinking about suicide, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) at any time. In a life-threatening emergency, call 911. To talk with King Health Systems about care, call 410-578-4340.
